title: No Nails, No Glue: How Dougong Holds Up a Chinese Roof | China Travel Expert
description:
Watch a Chinese bracket set — dougong (斗拱) — go up block by block, no nails and no glue anywhere.

A big wooden block (櫨斗 lúdǒu) sits on the column. Bow-shaped arms (拱 gǒng) drop into its notches, small blocks (散斗 sàndǒu) ride on their ends, and a slanted lever (昂 áng) reaches out to catch the eave. Nothing is bolted or pinned: every joint is held by friction and the weight of the roof pressing down. Stack a few of these and the load fans outward before it travels down the column — and when the ground shakes, the joints flex instead of snapping. That is why China's oldest timber halls, like the East Hall of Foguang Temple (857) and the all-wood Yingxian Pagoda (1056), are still standing.

🧭 Expert Tip: Next time you're under an old Chinese eave, look straight up — the stack of interlocking blocks fanning out from the column is dougong.

斗拱：无钉无胶，全靠摩擦和屋顶自重咬合；受力层层外展再下传，地震时关节能活动——这就是佛光寺东大殿、应县木塔千年不倒的原因。
